---
title: "Quiz: thresholds from noise statistics"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. "$k$" is a threshold in units of the noise standard deviation of the filtered image.

---

**Q1.** Why is a threshold in units of noise better than a threshold on raw grey values?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What changes when the exposure doubles?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Raw values change with exposure, gain, camera, illumination and the filter used; the same number means a different thing on every image. Dividing by the noise makes $k$ a statement about probabilities ("how unusual is this for noise?"), which carries over between images and filters.
:::

---

**Q2.** The pixel values of a background region are $(4, -2, 1, 0, 30, -1, 2, -3, 0)$. Estimate the noise with the MAD. What would the ordinary standard deviation say?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Median first, then the median of the absolute deviations, then divide by 0.6745.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Sorted: $-3, -2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 30$, median 0. Absolute deviations sorted: $0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 30$, median 2. $\hat\sigma = 2/0.6745 = 2.97$. The ordinary standard deviation is 10.2, dominated by the single value 30 (a spot, not noise).
:::

---

**Q3.** A pixel of pure noise exceeds 3 sd with probability 0.13 %. Why does a 512 × 512 image filtered at σ = 1.5 give about 100 false spots at $k = 3$, not 0.13 % of its maxima (about 6)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which pixels does the detector test?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The detector tests only local maxima, and a local maximum is the largest value of its neighbourhood: its distribution is shifted to higher values than that of an ordinary pixel. So the fraction of maxima above 3 sd is far larger than 0.13 % (about 2 %, 99 of 4 862).
:::

---

**Q4.** At $k = 4$ a 512² image has about 4 false spots. How many do you expect in a 2048² image with the same filter and threshold? What $k$ would bring it back to about 4?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
False spots scale with the area. From $k = 4$ to $k = 5$ the count drops by about a factor 40.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
16 times the area: about $16 \times 4.3 \approx 69$. To get back to about 4 per image, raise $k$ to about 4.7 (the Euler formula gives 4.4 false spots per 2048² image at $k = 4.7$). Bigger images need slightly higher thresholds for the same number of false spots per image.
:::

---

**Q5.** With $k = 4$, noise sd 10 and spots of σ = 1.5, what is roughly the dimmest spot (peak amplitude) you can detect? What changes if you collect four times more light?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$A_\text{min} \approx k\sigma_n/\sqrt{\pi\sigma^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$40/\sqrt{\pi \cdot 2.25} = 40/2.66 \approx 15$ grey levels above the background. With four times the light, every spot's signal is ×4 but the shot noise only ×2: all SNRs double, so spots half as bright as before (relative to the new exposure) now reach the threshold.
:::

---

**Q6.** An image has Poisson noise and a bright region. With one global threshold, where do the false spots appear, and where are spots missed? Name two fixes.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Variance = mean.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The noise sd is larger where the background is bright. A global threshold (set from the typical, mostly dark, pixels) is too low there, so false spots cluster in the bright region; in dark regions it is too high relative to the local noise, so dim spots are missed. Fixes: a local noise estimate $\sqrt{\text{gain} \cdot \text{background} + \text{read noise}^2}$ per pixel, or the Anscombe transform $2\sqrt{x + 3/8}$ before filtering.
:::

---

**Q7.** Your camera adds a faint fixed stripe pattern, and you measure the noise with the MAD on the raw image. After filtering you get more false spots than predicted. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\sqrt{\sum w^2}$ assumes independent pixels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The stripes make the noise correlated: the filter averages independent noise down, but a pattern that is smooth along the stripes survives averaging. The predicted filtered noise $\hat\sigma\sqrt{\sum w^2}$ is then too small, and the threshold too low. Estimate the noise on the filtered image itself (or on blank images taken with the same camera).
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that the median of $|X - \mu|$ for $X \sim \mathcal N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is $0.6745\,\sigma$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$P(|Z| \le c) = 2\Phi(c) - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The median $m$ satisfies $P(|X - \mu| \le m) = \tfrac12$, i.e. $2\Phi(m/\sigma) - 1 = \tfrac12$, so $\Phi(m/\sigma) = 0.75$ and $m = \Phi^{-1}(0.75)\,\sigma = 0.6745\,\sigma$.
:::
